title: Format String Foothold
description: A remote format-string exploitation exercise, following all six tasks of SEED Labs' Format String Attack Lab against the lab's own format.c/server.c.
prerequisites: Comfortable with the Linux command line and basic C (pointers, the stack).
outcomes: Identify, leak through, write through, and exploit a format-string vulnerability, understand the 64-bit zero-byte-address constraint, and fix the underlying bug.

levels.title: Introduction
levels.content:
# General information

* This game is for educational purposes only.
* The solution of a level is required for later levels.

# Storyline

A remote server has a format-string vulnerability in how it handles user input (`printf(msg)` instead of `printf("%s", msg)`). Your job: crash it, read its memory, write to its memory, inject code into it, and finally help fix it.

This follows all six tasks of SEED Labs' *Format String Attack Lab* (W. Du) — see ATTRIBUTION.txt.

# Before you start

The server sends its output back to you on a **second** connection, not on the same one you used to send your request: before connecting to `10.1.26.20:9090`, start a listener on your own machine's port **9091** (e.g. `nc -lvp 9091`), in a separate terminal, to receive it. Every level from here on assumes you're doing this.

levels.title: Get Access
levels.cloud_content:
Access the sandbox, then submit **`start`**.

### Sandbox access
1. In the topology overview, right-click **`attacker`** and click **`Open GUI`**.
2. Login with username **`user`** and password **`Password123`**.

See [documentation](https://docs.platform.cyberrange.cz/user-guide-advanced/sandboxes/sandbox-access/#user-access) for SSH access.
levels.local_content: This sandbox has not been tested for use with local sandbox.

levels.title: Recon
levels.content:
Scan `server` (10.1.26.20) and find the one listening TCP service.

The flag is the port number.

levels.title: Task 1: Crashing the Program
levels.content:
With a listener on 9091 running, send a benign line (e.g. `hello`) to `10.1.26.20:9090` and note the final line you receive back on 9091.

Then send input containing several `%s` format specifiers instead, and compare: the program's stdout is fully buffered when it's writing to a socket rather than a terminal, so when it crashes before exiting normally, none of that buffered output (including the final line) ever gets flushed — you'll likely get nothing back on 9091 at all, which is itself the confirmation.

The flag is the exact final line that appears after a benign request but never after a crashing one.
levels.solution:
```
$ printf 'hello' | nc 10.1.26.20 9090      # on 9091: ... (^_^)(^_^)  Returned properly (^_^)(^_^)
$ printf '%s%s%s%s%s%s%s%s%s%s%s%s' | nc 10.1.26.20 9090   # on 9091: nothing at all
```
Each %s tells printf to dereference the next stack value as a pointer; most aren't valid, and the process segfaults before main() can print its final line — or anything else still sitting in the unflushed stdout buffer.

hints.title: Why does this crash?
hints.content: Each %s tells printf to dereference the next stack value as a pointer; most aren't valid.

levels.title: Task 2: Printing Out the Server's Memory
levels.content:
**2.A — Stack data.** The banner (on 9091) already gives you the input buffer's address directly — you don't need to brute-force it with a marker the way the SEED handout's generic walkthrough does. What you still need to find is the **offset**: how many `%x` (or which `%N$x`) specifiers it takes before the output matches the address you were just given, confirming that position on the argument pointer corresponds to the very start of your own input.

**2.B — Heap data.** Using that offset with `%N$s` instead of `%N$x`, and the secret message's address (also in the banner) placed little-endian at the start of your payload, leak its contents.

See SEED Labs handout, section 4.

The flag is the secret string revealed in 2.B.

hints.title: Finding your offset (2.A)
hints.content: Send a unique marker followed by several %N$x and look for which N echoes it back — or echoes the buffer address from the banner.

hints.title: Byte order (2.B)
hints.content: x86-64 is little-endian when packing an address into your payload.

levels.title: Task 3: Modifying the Server's Memory
levels.content:
Use `%n` with the offset from Task 2 to write to a chosen address instead of reading from it — target the `target` variable, whose address is also in the banner.

**3.A** — change `target` to any different value, to confirm the write works at all.
**3.B** — change it to exactly `0x5000`.
**3.C** — for a larger target value (e.g. `0xAABBCCDD`), use `%hn` or `%hhn` instead of a plain `%n`, so you don't need printf to emit billions of padding characters first.

See SEED Labs handout, section 5.

The flag is the line the server prints once `target` reads back as exactly `0x5000` (3.B) — the program always prints it zero-padded to 16 hex digits.

hints.title: Controlling the byte count (3.B)
hints.content: A width-padded conversion like %050d lets you set printf's running output-byte-count before the %n.

hints.title: Four/eight bytes is a lot (3.C)
hints.content: %hn / %hhn write 2 / 1 bytes at a time, reaching a large target without huge padding.

levels.title: Task 4: Inject Malicious Code
levels.content:
Combine the read and write primitives from Tasks 2-3 to overwrite a saved return address with the address of shellcode placed inside your own input (the stack is executable). See SEED Labs handout, section 6, and section 9 for turning it into a reverse shell.

Objective: achieve code execution as the `formatsvc` account and read `flag_task3.txt` from its home directory.

This exercise does not ship a ready-made exploit payload or shellcode — build and test one against a provisioned sandbox using the offsets you found in Tasks 2-3.
levels.solution: See SEED Labs handout, sections 6 and 9.

hints.title: Where does the shellcode go?
hints.content: Anywhere in your own input, at a known offset you can compute an address for.

hints.title: What do you overwrite?
hints.content: The saved return address of the function printf() is running inside.

levels.title: Task 5: Attacking the 64-bit Server
levels.content:
This sandbox's target is already a 64-bit binary, so you solved this task's core problem while building Task 4: on x86-64 Linux, user-space addresses never use their top two bytes, which means every address you place in your payload contains at least two `0x00` bytes. Since `printf()` stops reading its format string at the first `\0`, you cannot simply paste such an address into the middle of your payload and keep going — anything after that zero byte is ignored.

Explain, in your own words, which part of your Task 4 payload could not simply contain a raw address followed by more format-string text, and how the `%N$` positional-parameter syntax (used throughout Tasks 2-4) sidesteps the problem by letting you place every address at the very start of the buffer instead.

The flag is: how many of the 8 bytes in a typical x86-64 user-space address are always `0x00`?
levels.solution: Two. Addresses above 0x00007FFFFFFFFFFF are not valid user-space addresses on x86-64 Linux, so the top two bytes of every address you leak or construct are always zero — which is exactly why every address in this exercise's payloads has to sit at the very start of the buffer (via %N$ positional parameters), never in the middle followed by more text.

hints.title: Where do the zero bytes come from?
hints.content: x86-64 Linux user-space addresses top out around 0x00007FFFFFFFFFFF.

levels.title: Task 6: Fixing the Problem
levels.content:
`gcc` warns about the vulnerable `printf(msg)` call at compile time by default. Build `format.c` and read the warning.

Fix the vulnerability (pass the user's input as a `%s` argument instead of as the format string itself), recompile, and confirm your Task 1 payload no longer crashes the program.

The flag is the name of the compiler warning flag gcc reports for this specific mistake (format: `-W...`).
levels.solution: `-Wformat-security`. The fix is to change `printf(msg)` to `printf("%s", msg)` — after that, every `%` character in the input is just a literal character again, and the warning disappears on rebuild.

hints.title: Where's the warning?
hints.content: It appears during compilation, pointing at the printf(msg) line.
